rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. Starting at 40 °C leaves room to adjust temperature in either direction for selectivity.
Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the critical pair responds to slope. The last peak should remain near or below 10 minutes, leaving room to improve resolution without a time penalty.

The critical pair improves with a shallower gradient. Raising the starting organic fraction while extending the gradient should provide additional separation without pushing the last peak much beyond 10 minutes; the scouting run suggests sufficient retention remains for the earliest peak.
Injection 3 attained the maximum CRF. Raise temperature by one grid step to seek a shorter fully resolved run while testing whether the critical pair retains R ≥ 1.5.

The critical pair moved sharply toward co-elution at 45 °C; testing 55 °C may separate it again after an elution-order reversal and shorten the run. Retain injection 3 as the maximum-score fallback while checking for new critical pairs.

Slightly flatten the gradient at 55 °C to try to resolve the new critical pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. Monitor the other close pair as well, since its reversed elution order may make it respond oppositely to gradient slope.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten the fully resolved 55 °C method while slightly flattening its gradient. Check that the earliest pair remains retained and that both critical pairs preserve R ≥ 1.5.

Lowering the starting organic fraction should improve the pair that deteriorated at phi0 = 0.20, potentially allowing a shorter gradient. Test whether 14 minutes preserves both critical separations while reducing the last-peak time relative to injection 6.
Shorten injection 8 by one gradient-time step to seek a faster maximum-score method. This directly tests whether its two closest pairs retain baseline resolution under modest compression.

Reduce the endpoint to flatten the 12-minute gradient enough to recover the critical pair's resolution, targeting a last-peak time between injections 8 and 9. The last peak previously eluted near 0.57 organic, so an endpoint of 0.85 leaves ample elution strength.
Use a slightly steeper gradient than injection 10 to shorten elution while aiming to retain R ≥ 1.5 for both critical pairs. The 0.75 endpoint remains comfortably above the observed elution window.

Explore a faster, hotter regime that may separate the temperature-sensitive pair after an elution-order reversal. This is a selectivity test rather than a small refinement; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test whether a steeper gradient increases separation of the newly reversed critical pair at 60 °C while substantially shortening elution. Monitor its neighboring pairs for compression; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Explore low-temperature selectivity with a shorter gradient, since the hot, steep gradients leave multiple unresolved pairs. Cooling may separate the central cluster in a different order; the strong endpoint limits the risk of excessive late retention.

Test whether a lower starting organic fraction restores the unresolved pair from injection 9 while retaining its short gradient. This also checks whether the other close pair loses too much resolution as the starting fraction decreases.

Test intermediate low-temperature selectivity with a shorter gradient than the fully resolved 40 °C method. Cooling may improve its temperature-sensitive critical pair, but the neighboring separations must be checked; injection 15 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Slightly steepen the fastest confirmed fully resolved method to test its time limit on the available grid. The endpoint remains above the elution window, but the two critical pairs have little resolution margin and must be checked.

Return to the fully resolved 40 °C regime and raise the starting organic fraction one step to seek earlier elution. This tests a different route to shortening the run while checking both early retention and the temperature-sensitive central pair.

Test the remaining intermediate-temperature regime with a fast gradient, looking for favorable separation after the central pair changes order. Keep injection 15 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score fallback.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction and steeper gradient improve the reversed central pair at 50 °C while shortening elution. Check early-pair resolution carefully; injection 15 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Trim injection 15's unused high-organic segment while preserving its starting composition, temperature, and gradient slope. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends, retaining maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Refine around injection 6 to seek a maximum-score method with more balanced resolution margins than the fastest methods. This slightly shallower gradient should keep both critical pairs near R = 1.7 and the last peak below 10 minutes.

Test a gradient slope just steeper than injection 11, targeting a shorter fully resolved run near the critical pair’s resolution boundary. Injection 15 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method if this small increase drops R below 1.5.

Interpolate between injections 5 and 6 to shorten the better-resolved 55 °C method while targeting both critical pairs above R = 1.5. This should retain maximum CRF with more resolution margin than the fastest confirmed method.

Trim injection 10 to an eight-minute gradient while preserving its slope, starting composition, and temperature. Its last peak should still elute before the gradient ends, retaining maximum CRF and slightly more minimum-resolution margin than the fastest confirmed method.
